html:
A famine in north China from 1876 to 1879, caused by years of drought, that killed somewhere between 9.5 and 13 million people. Shanxi province was hit hardest, with millions of deaths, followed by Zhili (Hebei), Henan and Shandong.

Rains failed from 1875, linked to a strong El Niño that brought drought to India and Brazil at the same time, as in the Great Famine in India. Crops failed year after year. Shanxi was inland and mountainous, with poor roads, so grain could not get in. People ate bark and grass, sold children, and there were reports of cannibalism.

The Qing government did send relief, and raised money by selling official titles, but it was not enough. Its funds and attention were also tied up in reconquering Xinjiang. Foreign missionaries, such as the Welshman Timothy Richard, ran relief too, and the disaster drew international appeals.

The famine pushed many survivors to move north into Manchuria, part of the long migration called Chuang Guandong.
